newsitem.title: GERMANY: German leaders quickly slam Euro critic Schroeder.
newsitem.headline: German leaders quickly slam Euro critic Schroeder.

text.p: Finance Minister Theo Waigel and Chancellery Minister Friedrich Bohl denounced on Sunday an opposition leader who predicted the single European currency euro would be weaker than the mark.

Gerhard Schroeder, premier of Lower Saxony and a leading chancellor candidate for the opposition Social Democrats (SPD), said in an interview in the news weekly Focus on Saturday that "naturally the euro will be weaker than the mark".

Schroeder also stirred fears that Germany would end up supporting weaker European countries after the euro is introduced and lamented the fact that anyone who raises such concerns in Germany is quickly labelled anti-European.
Blistering criticisms rained down on Schroeder only a few hours later, with Waigel slamming him for resorting to populist arguments and Bohl lambasting Schroeder for his "irresponsible" remarks.
"He is proving once again with his reckless comments that he doesn't let any opportunity pass to get voters worked up with populism," Waigel told Welt am Sonntag newspaper on Sunday.
"Once again this is nothing more than his obsession in raising his own political profile," Waigel added.

Chancellery Minister Bohl said Schroeder should worry more about reducing budget deficits in his own state and help Germany qualify for the single European currency in 1999 rather than stir fears among the public.

"Schroeder's panic-mongering against the euro is entirely irresponsible," Bohl told Welt am Sonntag. "The European economic and monetary union will most importantly be a motor for growth from which Germany will especially profit."

Schroeder even ran into immediate criticism from another SPD leader, premier of Rhineland Palatinate Kurt Beck, who said this was not the right time to add new irritations to the existing confusion in the German population over the euro.

After suffering losses in state elections in March for their earlier flirtation with Euro-scepticism, the SPD has in recent months reversed its position on the euro and said the single currency is the best response to a dominant dollar.

But Schroeder, who regularly stands up well against Kohl in voter surveys and is the SPD candidate many say would pose the most serious threat to Kohl's hopes for reelection in 1998, said he would not stay quiet on an issue that worries many Germans.

"Naturally the euro will be weaker than the mark," Schroeder said. "If you put several weak currencies together with a few that are very strong, an absolutely strong currency cannot come out of that."

A survey by the INRA polling institute found 54 percent of Germans surveyed felt the euro would bring them disadvantages while only 30 percent saw advantages. Other surveys find about two-thirds of the Germans oppose trading the mark for the euro. 291021 GMT dec 96
